perStory.premise: A city wakes up one day to discover every person's
perStory.text:
The change came at 4:12 on a Tuesday morning, though nobody in Halvorsen City agreed on that later. What people agreed on was the color: a faint amber shimmer above the head, like heat off asphalt, and inside it the words, moving.

Ruth Abaya, who drove the 6 AM 44 bus down Cordell Avenue, was the first person she knew of to see it. She had stopped at a light and glanced at the man crossing in front of her, a man in a suit carrying a cake box, and above him she read: *don't drop it don't drop it don't drop it she'll cry if you drop it.* She sat through the green light. Behind her, horns. Above the horns, in amber: *MOVE*, and *what is wrong with her*, and from the car three back, *I think my father is dying and I have to go to work anyway.*

By seven the city had stopped functioning in the ordinary way. Not because of chaos — there was less shouting than you'd expect — but because everyone was reading. People stood in intersections with their heads tipped back like tourists. The financial district emptied itself out onto the sidewalks. A woman in a gray coat sat down on the steps of the courthouse and did not get up for four hours, because everyone who passed her was a novel.

The predicted catastrophes mostly did not happen. Some did. Three marriages ended before noon on Ashfield Street alone. A city councilman was found in his car with the engine running and the garage door open, which was the mercy in it. But the great fear — that the city would tear itself apart over what it learned — didn't quite arrive, and afterward people argued about why.

Ruth had a theory. She'd spent eleven years watching faces come up the steps of her bus, and she had always assumed she knew what was behind them: irritation, mostly, and impatience with her, and the low contempt that people have for the person operating the machine they're stuck inside. That's what the faces said. But that first morning, as they filed on and paid and looked at her, she read: *she has kind eyes*, and *is that the same driver from before, I like her*, and *God I hope I remembered to lock the door*, and *my back hurts*, and *my back hurts*, and *my back hurts.*

Almost nobody was thinking about her at all. And the ones who were, were thinking something soft.

That was the thing that nobody had prepared for. Everyone had braced for the cruelty and the lust and the petty math of judgment, and yes, all of it was there, amber and shameless above every head in the city — *she's gotten heavy*, *he's an idiot*, *I want*, *I want*, *I want.* But it turned out that cruelty was a smaller share of the total than anyone had feared, and that it was almost never the main thing, and that it passed. A man would think something vicious about the woman next to him on the platform and then, eleven seconds later, think about a dog he'd had in 1994. The vicious thought had felt, from the inside, like a verdict. From the outside it looked like weather.

What people could not get used to — what broke them, when they broke — was the loneliness. The sheer volume of it, hanging over the crowd like smog. *Nobody knows this about me. Nobody knows this about me. Nobody knows this about me*, ten thousand people thinking it at once in the same station, each one certain of it, each one wrong.

It lasted nine days. When it stopped, the city went strange and quiet for a week, and then, mostly, back to normal. People stopped talking about it. There was a period where strangers were unbearably gentle with each other and then that faded too, the way it does.

But Ruth kept a habit from it. When somebody came up the steps of her bus, hunched, avoiding her eyes, she made a point of saying good morning, out loud, every time — because she had read the smog and she knew exactly what was in it, and she knew that saying anything at all cut a small hole in it, and that the hole closed fast.

perStory.premise: The world's luck is finite, and someone has begun
perStory.text:
The lottery in Hesperia County was won three hundred and eleven consecutive times by tickets purchased at a gas station off Route 9, which is where Delia Ostrander started, because that is where the actuaries start when the numbers break.

She was not an actuary. She had been one, for eleven years, and then she had been the woman who noticed the shape in the data and would not stop saying so at meetings, and then she had been unemployed. Now she kept a ledger. In it she recorded, in a hand that had grown small and careful, every improbability she could verify: the four aircraft that landed after total hydraulic failure in a single April; the eight children pulled unhurt from a collapsed school in Novgorod; the man in Lisbon who survived a fall from the eleventh floor onto a parked van and walked away complaining about his hat.

The good luck was clustering. That was the first thing. Luck, properly understood, is a fine dust that settles evenly, and this had begun to drift — into certain rooms, certain postal codes, certain names.

The second thing was the debt.

Because the school in Novgorod had collapsed. Because the aircraft had lost their hydraulics in the first place. Because for every miracle in her ledger there was a page facing it, and on that page were the things that had never used to happen: the bridge in Ohio that failed on a windless Tuesday, inspected the month before, every bolt within tolerance. The pediatric ward in Cardiff where four separate machines stopped in four separate rooms in the same hour, and no engineer could find a fault in any of them, because there was no fault. There was only an absence of the thing that usually makes machines keep working, which nobody has a name for, and which everyone relies on.

The gas station off Route 9 had a clerk named Emil who was seventy-two and had a cough.

"Same fella," he said. "Every Tuesday. Buys one ticket, hands it to whoever's in line behind him. Never keeps it."

"And they win."

"Every time." Emil laughed, and the laugh turned into the cough, and the cough went on a while. "Figured he was some kind of saint."

Delia waited three Tuesdays. On the third, a thin man in a grey coat came in at 4:40, bought a single ticket, and turned to hand it to her.

She did not take it.

"How much have you moved?" she asked.

He lowered his hand. Up close he looked tired in a way that had nothing to do with sleep — the tiredness of something running at a loss for a very long time.

"You're the one with the notebook," he said.

"I'm the one with the notebook."

"Then you already know it isn't stealing." He set the ticket on the counter. "It was never distributed fairly. It pooled. It sat in vaults and bloodlines and it did nothing. Some families have been drawing on inherited fortune for two hundred years and calling it character. I only opened the valves."

"The ward in Cardiff."

"Yes."

"Four children."

"Yes." He said it without flinching, which was worse than flinching. "And eight in Novgorod. And nineteen on the ferry at Kos, and the crew of the Sofia Marie, and I have every one of them written down too, in a book like yours but longer. I am not pretending it's free. I'm saying the ledger was always running. Someone was always paying. The only thing I changed was who."

Delia looked at the ticket on the counter. Outside, the light was going the particular orange of late autumn, and somewhere in the world, she understood, a coin was landing wrong for someone who had never asked to be part of the arithmetic.

"You can't decide that," she said.

"No," he agreed. "But it was being decided. It was just being decided by nobody, which everyone had agreed to call fair."

He went out. The bell over the door rang, and the door caught on the frame, and stuck, the way doors do.

Delia stood in the fluorescent hum with the ticket in front of her and did not touch it, and behind her Emil coughed, and coughed, and then stopped.

perStory.premise: Every dream leaves behind a physical object by mor
perStory.text:
The lamp came first, on the morning after Mara's mother died.

It was a brass thing with a green glass shade, sitting on the kitchen floor beside the refrigerator where nothing had been the night before. She recognized it before she remembered dreaming it: the lamp from the hall of the house in Ellsworth, the one her mother read under, the one that had been sold at an estate sale in 1998 for eleven dollars.

She did not tell anyone. This was the first mistake, or possibly the only correct decision she ever made.

The objects came every night after that. A dinner plate with a hairline crack. A blue hair elastic. Half a bicycle, sheared clean down the seat tube, the pedal still turning slightly when she found it in the bathtub. Some mornings the object was small enough to fit in her palm — a pill, a stone, a molar. Some mornings she had to open the front door and stand in the yard and reckon with a thing the size of a boat.

She learned that other people had this too, once she started paying attention. It was in the way strangers apologized for the smell of chlorine on them, or carried a folding table nobody had asked them to bring. The city had a whole department for it. Two men in gray came with a truck, on Tuesdays, and took away whatever you left at the curb, and never once asked what any of it was. That was the mercy of the arrangement. Nobody asked.

But there were people who kept them. Mara met one at a party, a man named Devlin who had a storage unit in Revere and drove out to it on Sundays. He described it the way other men describe boats.

"Fourteen years," he said. "Every single one."

"What's it like?"

"Loud," he said, and laughed, and did not explain.

She thought about that for a long time. She had been leaving hers at the curb — the plates, the elastic, the enormous folded map of a city with no name, the sixty-three identical teacups from the week she had the flu. Every Tuesday the gray truck took them. And every Tuesday she felt something in her chest go a little quieter, a little further away, and she had assumed that was healing.

In March she dreamed of nothing she could remember, and woke to find a small wooden box on the pillow beside her, warm as bread.

Inside was a note in her mother's handwriting. It said: *Don't forget to eat something.*

She read it eleven times. Then she put it back in the box and put the box in the closet, and did not put it at the curb, and that Tuesday she stood at the window watching the gray truck take the rest and felt, for the first time in months, something like a hand on the back of her neck.

She started keeping them after that. Not all — she was not Devlin, she had a one-bedroom — but the ones that came with weight. She built a shelf. The lamp came back to her, or a lamp like it, and she plugged it in and it worked, and she read under it at night the way her mother had, and understood that she was dreaming forward as much as back.

In the fall she met a woman named June who worked at a bakery and had, on her forearm, a small tattoo of a key.

"That's a strange thing to get," Mara said.

"It's not a tattoo," June said. "It's a dream. Some of them come out on you instead of on the floor. Nobody knows why."

"What does it open?"

June looked at her with an expression Mara would spend the next several years trying to describe to herself, and failing.

"I've been waiting eleven years to find out," she said. "But I keep the door."

They were married the following spring. On the morning after the wedding Mara woke to find, on the floor at the foot of the bed, an ordinary door, unattached to any wall, standing upright and perfectly balanced, with a lock in it.

June was already awake, sitting up, holding her own arm, saying nothing.

Neither of them moved for a long time. Outside, it was Tuesday, and the gray truck was coming up the street, and they let it pass.

perStory.premise: A mountain slowly walks across the continent once
perStory.text:
The mountain's name, in the language of the people who had lived longest at its foot, was simply Grandmother, and for nine hundred and ninety-two years it had been a mountain like any other. Basalt shoulders. A cap of snow that thinned each summer and never quite vanished. Goats on the western scree. A road that switchbacked up to a pass where the wind made a sound like a woman clearing her throat.

Ilsa Verrant had spent eleven years measuring it.

Her instruments were bolted into bedrock at forty stations, and every one of them said the same thing, which was nothing. The mountain sat. Rock does creep — glaciers of stone, whole ranges sagging a millimeter a century under their own weight — but that was not walking, and Ilsa had not come here for that.

She had come because of the ditches.

They ran across the plain to the east, eight of them, parallel and enormous, silted to the brim and grown over with saltbush so that from the ground they were merely a stripe of greener scrub. From the air they were unmistakable: a track, four kilometers wide, running west-northwest for eleven hundred kilometers, terminating at Grandmother's eastern flank. The geological survey called them relict fluvial channels. Ilsa had spent a year proving they were not. Water does not carry basalt boulders uphill. Water does not leave a trench with a bottom pressed flat and glassy, the mineral grains flowed and refrozen the way sand fuses under a great and patient weight.

Someone had asked her, at a conference, what she thought had made them.

"A foot," she said.

She did not go back to that conference.

The local histories were no help and every kind of help. There were songs about Grandmother going to visit her sister, which the ethnographers had catalogued as a fertility motif, and there was a particular grammatical construction in the old dialect — a tense used only for things that happen once in a life you will not live to see twice. It was applied to three subjects: the great flood, a certain comet, and the mountain's traveling.

Ilsa's calculations, done badly at first and then very carefully, put the interval at 1,014 years and the last event at 1,009 years ago, plus or minus a decade she could not narrow.

She told no one. She wrote grant applications about slope stability.

In the autumn of the eleventh year, the goats left. Not dramatically — they simply were not there, and the herders said the animals had gone down to the low pastures early and would not be driven back. Then the springs on the north face ran cloudy. Then, in November, every one of Ilsa's forty stations recorded, simultaneously, a rotation of eight-thousandths of a degree.

It took eleven months to complete the first step.

There was no thunder. There was no cracking open of the earth. The village at the foot had four seasons' warning and the villagers, who had been told by their grandmothers and had believed it the way one believes in a distant war, moved their houses two valleys over with the unhurried competence of people following a plan drafted long ago. The road's switchbacks stretched and then failed, the pass migrating northward at the speed of a fingernail growing.

Ilsa stayed. She camped on the moraine and watched the horizon change by degrees too small to see and too large to argue with, and she understood, sometime in the second year, that she had been asking the wrong question. Not *how*. Not even *why*. The question was what it meant that a thing could move so slowly that the only creatures capable of noticing were the ones who wrote things down, and that this — the writing down, the eleven years of instruments, the tense reserved for the once-seen — was perhaps the only reason the walking was witnessed at all.

Grandmother would arrive somewhere, in four centuries or six. Ilsa would not see it. Her data would, if anyone kept it.

She built a cairn on the moraine, and cut into the largest stone the date, and the bearing, and a single sentence in the old dialect, in the tense for things you see once.

Then she went down to the low pastures, where the goats were, and where the light in the evening came from a direction that was, very gradually, no longer quite the same.

perStory.premise: Memories can be planted like gardens.
perStory.text:
The greenhouse smelled like wet clay and something faintly electrical, an ozone edge that Ilse had stopped noticing years ago but which made new clients wrinkle their noses.

"You want to see them first," she said. It wasn't a question. They always wanted to see them first.

The man — Petrov, fifty-something, hands that had never done outdoor work — nodded and followed her down the center aisle. Trays stretched away on either side under grow lights, each one holding rows of small pale shoots in a medium that looked like gray sand and wasn't.

"That's it?" he said. "They look like onions."

"They look like nothing. That's the point." Ilse stopped at a tray marked in her own handwriting: *B. — grandmother, kitchen, winter.* She lifted a seedling free. The root system came with it, finer than hair, trailing a filament network that caught the light. "The visible part is the scaffolding. What matters is underneath, and underneath doesn't photograph well."

"How long?"

"Depends what you're growing. A single afternoon — a smell, a face, one conversation — that's six weeks. A childhood is four years and it doesn't take in most people." She set the seedling back. "You didn't say which."

Petrov looked at the trays instead of at her. "My wife. Twenty-two years. She died in March and I find I can't — " He stopped, restarted. "I remember that she laughed. I don't remember the sound."

Ilse had heard versions of this maybe three hundred times, and it had not yet stopped being the hardest part.

"I can't grow that," she said.

"You have a whole building of—"

"I can grow *a* laugh. I can grow something that will feel like remembering, that will arrive unbidden while you're doing dishes, that will be indistinguishable from the real thing in every way you can test." She folded her arms. "It won't be hers. There's no seed for hers. Whatever you plant will be built out of laughs you've heard, women you've known, what you expect a wife to sound like. It grows from what's already in the soil."

He was quiet a long moment. Down the aisle, a misting system hissed and cut off.

"Does anyone care?" he asked. "About the difference?"

"You will. For about a year." She started walking again and he followed. "The first months, you'll catch yourself noticing the seams — the laugh comes at the wrong moments, or it's a little too musical, or it never varies. Then the noticing fades. Memory doesn't have a mechanism for flagging its own forgeries. By year two you'll have folded it in with everything else and you won't be able to find the edge if you go looking."

"And that's bad."

"I didn't say bad." Ilse stopped at the end of the row, where a single tray sat apart from the others under a dimmed lamp, its shoots taller, silvering at the tips. "That's mine. Nine years old now. My mother telling me she was proud of me, on a Tuesday, in the car outside a swimming pool."

Petrov studied it. "Did she?"

"No. She died without saying it and I don't think she felt it, and for a long time that was a stone I carried around." She adjusted the lamp a quarter turn out of habit. "Now I have a Tuesday. The vinyl seats were hot. She had her sunglasses pushed up in her hair. I can tell you what the chlorine smelled like coming off my own skin."

"Is it enough?"

Ilse considered lying, the way she considered it every time, and found she still didn't have the stomach for it.

"It's not the same shape as the thing it replaced," she said. "The stone was heavy but it was hers — it came from her, it was evidence she'd existed a particular way. The Tuesday is light and warm and it came from me. Some days that's a mercy. Some days it feels like I paid a debt off with counterfeit money and the creditor was my mother."

She turned back toward the front of the greenhouse.

"Six weeks for a laugh," she said. "Think about it for two of them. The ones who don't think about it are the ones who come back."
